Three-dimensional DOP

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how sky directions constrain east, north, up and receiver clock at the same time.

A linearized pseudorange row in local east, north, up coordinates is Hᵢ = [−cosEᵢ sinAᵢ, −cosEᵢ cosAᵢ, −sinEᵢ, 1], where A is azimuth from north and E is elevation. The fourth parameter is receiver clock distance cb in metres.

With equal independent range errors of standard deviation σ, covariance is σ²Q, where Q = (HᵀH)⁻¹ when the geometry has full rank. HDOP = √(Qee + Qnn), VDOP = √Quu, TDOP = √Qbb, PDOP² = HDOP² + VDOP², and GDOP² = PDOP² + TDOP².

DOP values are dimensionless. The three-coordinate position RMS scale is σPDOP, while receiver-time standard deviation is σTDOP/c. Equal elevations make the height and clock columns proportional; more measurements at that same elevation cannot recover the missing distinction. The model reports rank loss rather than adding an artificial regularization.

Example

If a valid geometry has HDOP = 1 and VDOP = 2, PDOP = √5 ≈ 2.236. With TDOP = 1.5, GDOP = √7.25 ≈ 2.693. These values describe different combinations of position and clock uncertainty.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. Why can six measurements at exactly the same elevation fail to distinguish height error from clock error?

    Compare the up-column entries −sinE with the clock-column entries 1.

    Both columns are constant across measurements and therefore proportional. A suitable height change and clock-distance change produce the same common measurement effect, leaving the normal matrix rank deficient.

    2. If range-error σ doubles with sky geometry unchanged, what happens to DOP and to the position RMS scale?

    Separate Q from the multiplier σ² in covariance.

    DOP stays unchanged because it depends on geometry. The position RMS scale σPDOP doubles, and covariance multiplies by four.
